instruction.text: When she got to the Crimea, where do you think Mary Seacole built her hotel?

feedback.finish: Being close to the frontline was dangerous, but it meant that Mary could help the soldiers as quickly as possible.

instruction.text: You’re talking to Mary Seacole about her time in the Crimea. Fill in the gaps.

atoms.b: How did you set up your hotel?
atoms.sound: ssml: <prosody pitch = '-1st'>How did you set up your hotel</prosody>

atoms.b: I hired local workers to build it out of spare metal sheets and ((++wood glass)). It was not a very big structure, and you probably wouldn’t recognise it as a hotel!
Who came to your hotel in the Crimea?
atoms.sound: ssml: <prosody pitch = '-1st'>Who came to your hotel in the Crimea?</prosody>

atoms.b: We served food to British soldiers, gave them somewhere to ((++sleep play_tennis)) and looked after them very well. Many even called me Mother Seacole because I was so kind.
Did you help the soldiers out in other ways as well?
atoms.sound: ssml: <prosody pitch = '-1st'>Did you help the soldiers out in other ways as well?</prosody>

atoms.b: I sometimes rode out into battles to care for wounded ((++soldiers animals)) and comfort the dying.

instruction.text: What do you think it would have been like for Mary in the battles?

feedback.finish: When riding into battles, she was putting her own life at risk to care for the soldiers!

atoms.a: Mary Seacole’s hotel had a canteen and a restaurant.
Mary Seacole never went to the battlefields.
Mary Seacole was known as Mother Seacole in the Crimea.
